passages.t: ‘The sea observed and fled’: the exodus as a song
passages.happening:
Psalm 114 tells the whole story of the exodus in eight short verses. “When Israel departed from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of foreign tongue, Judah became God's sanctuary, and Israel His dominion” (verses 1 and 2).

Then nature reacts. “The sea observed and fled; the Jordan turned back; the mountains skipped like rams, the hills like lambs” (verses 3 and 4).

The poet turns and asks them why, as if teasing them. “Why was it, O sea, that you fled, O Jordan, that you turned back, O mountains, that you skipped like rams, O hills, like lambs?” (verses 5 and 6).

The answer comes as a command to the whole earth. “Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob, who turned the rock into a pool, the flint into a fountain of water!” (verses 7 and 8).
passages.hearers:
Each picture points to a story the hearers knew. The sea that fled is the Red Sea parting before Israel (Exodus 14:21-22). The Jordan that turned back is the river stopping so the people could cross into the land, forty years later (Joshua 3:16). The skipping mountains recall Mount Sinai, which “quaked violently” when God came down (Exodus 19:18). The rock that became a pool is the water God gave from the rock in the desert (Exodus 17:6).

So the psalm squeezes forty years into a few lines. It puts the start and the end of the story side by side: the sea at the beginning, the Jordan at the end.

Notice what is missing. God is not named until verse 7. The poet holds back the answer, letting us watch the sea run and the hills jump, before he says who made them do it.

A people ‘of foreign tongue’ (verse 1) means the Egyptians, whose speech the Israelites did not understand. Flint (verse 8) is the hardest stone in the desert, the last place anyone would look for water.

This psalm is part of the Hallel, as the note on Psalm 113 explains. At Passover, some sang it before the meal, retelling the exodus on the night that remembered it.
passages.later:
Habakkuk uses the same kind of picture: “The mountains saw You and quaked” (Habakkuk 3:10).

When Jesus calmed a storm, his frightened friends asked, “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?” (Mark 4:41). Psalm 114 had already shown the sea running from the God of Jacob.

Paul, thinking of the water from the rock in the desert, wrote that the Israelites “drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).
passages.asks:
Psalm 114 is playful and full of wonder. It asks you to see the great acts of God with fresh eyes, as if you were watching the hills jump.

It also says that God's presence changes things. Hard rock becomes a pool. Where in your life does the ground feel like flint? The psalm does not promise how God will act, but it reminds you who he is: the one who can bring water out of stone.
